script.opening: "This is embarrassing — I’ve had bad breath for ages and it’s knocking my confidence at work. Mints and mouthwash only mask it for a bit. I keep wondering if something’s wrong with my stomach. What’s actually causing it and how do I sort it?"

facts.text: About a year. "I can taste it, and I think people step back when I talk." His wife has mentioned it in the mornings. Worse in the morning and after coffee. Checks his breath many times a day.

Brushes once a day, sometimes twice; never cleans his tongue or between his teeth. Gums bleed when brushing. Hasn’t seen a dentist for about 4 years. If asked to look in his mouth on camera: tongue has a thick white-yellow coating at the back. No ulcers, no lumps he has noticed.

No blocked nose or post-nasal drip, no sore throat, no tonsil stones he knows of. No heartburn or acid, no swallowing problems, no weight loss. Not thirsty, not passing more urine. No dry mouth. Feels well.
Smokes 5 a day "socially". Drinks 4 coffees a day, a few beers at the weekend. Low-carb diet for the last 6 months to lose weight (only if asked about diet). No regular medicines. No allergies.
Sales manager — lots of face-to-face meetings. Married with one child. Avoids talking to people close up; it is "getting me down a bit". No low mood beyond that.

Embarrassed, a bit anxious. Convinced it’s your stomach: "So it’s not my stomach?" Accept the explanation if it makes sense. Agree to book a dentist this week. Ask about stopping the constant checking and worrying.

ice.ideas: "I thought it must be my stomach and maybe I need a test — a camera test or something for H. pylori."
ice.concerns: "I avoid talking to people close up. It’s getting me down." Worried it is affecting his chances of promotion.
ice.expectations: "A test to find the cause, and a treatment that actually works."

cues: "Is something wrong with my stomach?" — he expects a GI cause; explain that most bad breath starts in the mouth.
"It’s been a while since the dentist" (if asked) — dental review needed.
"I’m always checking" — possible anxiety about his breath to explore.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that most halitosis is ORAL in origin (oral hygiene, tongue coating, gum disease, caries, dry mouth) and takes an ORAL-FIRST approach (looking at the mouth, tongue and tonsils on video and asking about neck lumps) with a DENTAL check he books himself
Takes a history distinguishing TRUE from PERCEIVED halitosis (halitophobia) and covering oral care, ENT/GI symptoms, smoking, diet, dry mouth, drugs
Considers NON-ORAL causes where appropriate (ENT — sinusitis/post-nasal drip, tonsil stones; GI — GORD; smoking/diet/drugs)

Recognises SYSTEMIC red-flag causes with distinctive odours (DKA — ketotic, hepatic — fetor hepaticus, renal — uraemic) needing assessment, and NICE NG12 oral cancer features (ulcer over 3 weeks, persistent neck lump)

Manages with oral-hygiene optimisation (brushing, interdental and TONGUE cleaning, hydration, smoking/diet — OHID 2021), a self-booked dental check (chlorhexidine only short term: staining), and treatment of any identified ENT/GI cause
Addresses the embarrassment/confidence impact, reassures, and recognises/manages halitophobia where breath is objectively normal
Explores the impact on his confidence and relationships and any health anxiety behind the visit, and agrees the oral-first plan and dental review with him

Safety-nets and follows up: dental check, treat the cause, mouth ulcer over 3 weeks/neck lump/dysphagia, systemic red flags warranting assessment, and review — oral-first structured approach, not chasing a "stomach" cause

worked.txt: "It’s a really common thing to feel embarrassed about, and here’s the useful bit: most bad breath — the large majority of cases — actually comes from the mouth, not the stomach. Mouthwash just masks it, which is why it keeps coming back."
"Let me look in your mouth — the gums, teeth and especially the coating on the back of the tongue, which is a big source. How’s your oral hygiene and when did you last see a dentist?"

"The mainstays are brushing twice a day, cleaning between the teeth, and — importantly — cleaning your tongue with a scraper, plus staying well hydrated and easing off smoking and strong-smelling foods. And a proper dental check, because gum disease and decay are common causes — you can book directly with a dentist, or NHS 111 can help you find one."
"If your mouth’s healthy, I’d look at other causes — sinus problems or post-nasal drip, tonsil ‘stones’, or reflux from the stomach, which can contribute. We’d treat whichever fits."

"Rarely, certain medical conditions cause distinctive breath odours — I’ll just check you don’t have symptoms of things like diabetes, such as thirst or weight loss. But that’s uncommon. I’ll also check for mouth ulcers and feel your neck."

"Start with the oral hygiene and a dental visit — that fixes most cases. If your breath is actually fine and the worry persists, we can help with that too. Come back if it doesn’t improve and we’ll look further — and sooner if you get a mouth ulcer that doesn’t heal within three weeks, a lump in your neck, or trouble swallowing."

f.learning: Persistent HALITOSIS is approached oral-first, because the vast majority of true halitosis (most cases in published series) is ORAL in origin — poor oral hygiene, TONGUE coating, gingivitis/periodontal disease, dental caries/abscess and dry mouth — so the first step is an oral assessment and a DENTAL check-up that he books directly (GPs do not refer routinely), and patients (and clinicians) often over-attribute it to "the stomach" while mouthwash only masks it. Take a history distinguishing TRUE halitosis (confirmable, others notice) from PERCEIVED halitosis (HALITOPHOBIA — conviction of bad breath that is objectively normal, sometimes with anxiety/OCD features), covering oral care, ENT/GI symptoms, smoking, diet, dry mouth and medications. Where oral assessment is normal, consider non-oral causes: ENT (chronic sinusitis/post-nasal drip, tonsil stones/tonsilloliths, tonsillitis), GI (GORD — a recognised but over-attributed cause), respiratory infections, and drugs/smoking/diet. Recognise systemic/metabolic causes that are RED FLAGS with distinctive odours — diabetic ketoacidosis (ketotic/"pear-drop"), hepatic failure (fetor hepaticus) and renal failure (uraemic) — pointing to serious disease needing assessment. Manage by optimising oral hygiene (twice-daily brushing, interdental and tongue cleaning, hydration, reducing smoking/odorous foods), treating gum disease/caries via a self-booked dentist (the cornerstone; OHID Delivering better oral health 2021; chlorhexidine short term only, as it stains teeth), and treating any ENT/GI cause found; address the psychological/social impact and reassure, recognising and managing halitophobia (objectively normal breath → reassurance/psychological support) appropriately. NICE NG12: unexplained mouth ulceration for more than 3 weeks or a persistent unexplained neck lump needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer, so ask about and look for these (face to face if not clearly seen on video).

knowledge.summary: Most persistent bad breath comes from the mouth: the coating on the back of the tongue, gum disease, decay and a dry mouth. Start with the mouth, not the stomach. Look in the mouth, advise tongue cleaning and good oral hygiene, and ask him to see his dentist. Think about ENT and reflux causes if the mouth is healthy, recognise the rare systemic odours, and remember that some people are convinced of bad breath that others cannot detect.

points.t: Most true halitosis arises in the mouth, from bacteria on the back of the tongue, gingivitis or periodontitis, decay, food trapping and dry mouth. Mouthwash masks the smell briefly but does not treat the cause.

Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, spit rather than rinse, clean between the teeth, and see a dentist regularly [1]. Add gentle tongue cleaning. Stopping smoking improves gum health and breath [1].

Patients book NHS dental care directly; GPs do not refer routinely. Encourage a dental check for gum disease and decay. Chlorhexidine mouthwash can help gum inflammation short term but stains teeth and alters taste [4].

If the mouth is healthy, consider post-nasal drip and chronic rhinosinusitis, tonsil stones and tonsillitis, reflux [3], and chest infection or bronchiectasis. Drugs that dry the mouth and some foods (garlic, onion, alcohol) contribute.

Rare but important: a sweet, fruity smell with thirst and weight loss suggests ketoacidosis; fetor hepaticus suggests liver failure; a urine-like smell suggests kidney failure. NICE NG12: unexplained mouth ulceration lasting more than 3 weeks, or a persistent unexplained neck lump, needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for oral cancer [2].

Some people are sure they have bad breath when others notice nothing (halitophobia). Ask whether anyone has actually commented. Reassure with honesty, and explore anxiety, low mood or compulsive checking if the worry is out of proportion.

model.text: Hello, Mr Mehta, I’m Dr Shah. What can I help with today?

This is embarrassing. I’ve had bad breath for ages and it’s knocking my confidence at work. Mints and mouthwash only mask it for a bit. I keep wondering if something’s wrong with my stomach. What’s actually causing it and how do I sort it?
Thank you for bringing it up. It’s much more common than people think, and usually very treatable. I’ll ask some questions, have a look in your mouth on the camera, and then we’ll work out a plan.
Okay, good.
How do you know about the smell? Has someone mentioned it, or is it something you notice yourself?
I can taste it, and I think people step back when I talk. I’m always checking.
How do you look after your teeth, and when did you last see a dentist? Do you ever clean your tongue?
I brush, but I’ve never done anything with my tongue. It’s been a while since the dentist, to be honest.
Any bleeding gums, toothache, a dry mouth, or mouth ulcers that haven’t healed?
No ulcers. Nothing I’ve noticed.
What about your nose and throat: a blocked nose, catarrh running down the back of the throat, sore throats, or little white lumps on your tonsils?
Nothing like that.
And your stomach: heartburn, acid coming up, indigestion, or trouble swallowing?
Not really. I just assumed that’s where it comes from.
A few general questions. Have you been very thirsty, passing a lot of urine, or lost weight? Any cough bringing up phlegm?
No, I feel well in myself.
Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or take any tablets or medicines, including ones from the chemist?
No regular tablets. Nothing else I can think of.
You said it’s affecting your confidence. How is it affecting work and the rest of your life?
I avoid talking to people close up. It’s getting me down a bit. I thought it must be my stomach and maybe I need a test.
That sounds really hard. Thank you for telling me. Could you open wide and hold the phone light up so I can see your tongue, teeth and gums? Then I’ll explain.
There’s a coating on the back of your tongue. I can’t check your teeth and gums the way a dentist can, but I can see no ulcers or lumps, and your throat and neck feel normal.
model.why: Video oral inspection; neck by self-check

model.text: So it’s not my stomach?

Most likely not. In most people with bad breath, the cause is in the mouth: bacteria living in that tongue coating, and sometimes gum disease or decay. The stomach is a much less common cause, and you have no reflux symptoms. That’s why mouthwash only covers it up.
model.why: Explains the oral cause; addresses the stomach idea

model.text: That actually makes sense.

The good news is this is very fixable. Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between your teeth with floss or small brushes, and gently clean your tongue each day with a scraper or your brush. Would that fit into your routine?
model.why: Oral hygiene with tongue cleaning; checks feasibility

model.text: Yes, that’s easy enough.

Please also book a dental check-up, as gum disease and decay are common causes that only a dentist can properly check and treat. You can book directly with a dentist, or NHS 111 can help you find one.
model.why: Dental review, with how to access it

model.text: I’ll book one this week.

Drinking water through the day helps, and if you smoke or drink alcohol, cutting down helps your gums and breath too. If things aren’t better after the dental treatment, I’d look again at your nose, throat and stomach.
model.why: Lifestyle and a plan for non-oral causes

model.text: And the checking and worrying?
That’s important too. Once the cause is treated, many people find the worry fades. If you’re still feeling low or checking a lot, come back and we’ll talk about support for that.

Come back sooner if you get a mouth ulcer that doesn’t heal within three weeks, a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, or you become very thirsty or lose weight. Otherwise, see me in about six to eight weeks after the dentist.
model.why: NICE NG12 oral-cancer features, systemic features, planned review

model.text: Okay.
What will you do first when you get home?
Start cleaning my tongue and between my teeth, and book the dentist. Come back if I get an ulcer or lump or it doesn’t improve.
Exactly. This is common and treatable, and you’ve taken the right first step.

social.t: Bad breath can lead people to avoid close conversations, meetings and relationships. Ask how it affects daily life.
Finding an NHS dentist can be hard. NHS 111 and the NHS website can help locate one; NHS dental charges apply unless exempt.

legal.t: GPs are not trained to treat periodontal disease. Advise dental care rather than attempting dental treatment, and document the advice given.

professional.t: Patients often delay raising embarrassing symptoms. A respectful, matter-of-fact approach builds trust and may reveal anxiety or low mood.
Explaining why the stomach is unlikely, and why no endoscopy is needed, is safer than treating reflux he does not have.

community.t: Dental hygienists teach cleaning technique. Community pharmacists can advise on tongue cleaners, interdental brushes and dry-mouth products.

redFlags: Unexplained mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks or persistent neck lump: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Thirst, polyuria and a fruity smell (ketoacidosis); jaundice or confusion (liver failure)
psychosocial: Embarrassment and loss of confidence at work
ice: Concern: embarrassment and how others see him
Expectation: a test and a cure

playbook.diagnosis: “This is bad breath coming from your mouth, most likely the coating on your tongue, and the dentist will check for gum disease.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The back of the tongue is like a shag-pile carpet. Bacteria hide in it and give off smelly gases. Mouthwash is like air freshener; cleaning the tongue is like hoovering the carpet.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was your stomach and might need a test. From what I can see, it’s coming from your mouth, which is good news because it’s very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the embarrassment and its impact; offer support if the checking and low mood persist after treatment.
sharedPlan: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, spit don’t rinse; interdental cleaning (OHID 2021)
Dental check-up for gum disease and decay; book directly or through NHS 111
Water through the day; less smoking and alcohol if relevant
Reassess nose, throat and reflux if not improved after dental treatment
safetyNet: Return for a mouth ulcer lasting over 3 weeks, a neck lump, trouble swallowing, thirst or weight loss
Review in 6–8 weeks after dental care

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by chasing the stomach, by never looking in the mouth, and by missing the anxiety behind the visit. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Starting a PPI or requesting endoscopy for “stomach breath”.
items.why: Most halitosis is oral; he has no reflux or upper-GI symptoms.
items.fix: Look in the mouth first and explain the oral cause.

items.fail: Not looking at the tongue and gums or asking about the neck.
items.why: Tongue coating and gum disease are the common causes; an ulcer or neck lump would change the plan (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Look at tongue, gums, teeth, tonsils on video; ask her to feel her neck.

items.fail: Advising oral hygiene without mentioning the tongue or interdental cleaning.
items.why: Tongue coating is a major source and brushing alone misses it.
items.fix: Teach tongue and interdental cleaning alongside twice-daily brushing (OHID 2021).

items.fail: “See your dentist” with no idea how he will get an appointment.
items.why: Access is a real barrier; the advice may go nowhere.
items.fix: Explain he can book directly or use NHS 111 to find a dentist.

items.fail: Dismissing the problem because you cannot smell anything.
items.why: Misses real disease and the distress of halitophobia.
items.fix: Ask who has noticed it; explore checking and mood.

items.why: Non-healing ulcers or systemic symptoms need prompt action.
items.fix: Name the 3-week ulcer rule, neck lump, dysphagia, thirst and weight loss; review after dental care; teach-back.

avoid.instead: “Most bad breath starts in the mouth, so let’s start there.”
avoid.why: Oral causes dominate; endoscopy without upper-GI symptoms is unwarranted.

avoid.instead: “Cleaning your tongue and between your teeth treats the cause.”
avoid.why: Mouthwash masks the smell; chlorhexidine stains teeth with long use (BNF).

avoid.instead: “Let’s treat what I can see, and talk about the worry too.”

Oral halitosis, most likely from tongue coating; gum disease to be checked by a dentist.
Oral hygiene including tongue and interdental cleaning; dental check-up with guidance on access; lifestyle.
Plans reassessment for ENT or reflux causes if no improvement; addresses anxiety and checking.
Return for an ulcer lasting over 3 weeks, a neck lump, dysphagia, thirst or weight loss; review after dental care.

social.t: Bad breath can lead people to avoid close conversations, meetings and relationships. Ask how it affects daily life.
Finding an NHS dentist can be hard. NHS 111 and the NHS website can help locate one; NHS dental charges apply unless exempt.

legal.t: GPs are not trained to treat periodontal disease. Advise dental care rather than attempting dental treatment, and document the advice given.

professional.t: Patients often delay raising embarrassing symptoms. A respectful, matter-of-fact approach builds trust and may reveal anxiety or low mood.
Explaining why the stomach is unlikely, and why no endoscopy is needed, is safer than treating reflux he does not have.

community.t: Dental hygienists teach cleaning technique. Community pharmacists can advise on tongue cleaners, interdental brushes and dry-mouth products.

redFlags: Unexplained mouth ulcer lasting more than 3 weeks or persistent neck lump: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Thirst, polyuria and a fruity smell (ketoacidosis); jaundice or confusion (liver failure)
psychosocial: Embarrassment and loss of confidence at work
ice: Concern: embarrassment and how others see him
Expectation: a test and a cure

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is bad breath coming from your mouth, most likely the coating on your tongue, and the dentist will check for gum disease.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The back of the tongue is like a shag-pile carpet. Bacteria hide in it and give off smelly gases. Mouthwash is like air freshener; cleaning the tongue is like hoovering the carpet.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was your stomach and might need a test. From what I can see, it’s coming from your mouth, which is good news because it’s very treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge the embarrassment and its impact; offer support if the checking and low mood persist after treatment.
sharedPlan: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, spit don’t rinse; interdental cleaning (OHID 2021)
Dental check-up for gum disease and decay; book directly or through NHS 111
Water through the day; less smoking and alcohol if relevant
Reassess nose, throat and reflux if not improved after dental treatment
safetyNet: Return for a mouth ulcer lasting over 3 weeks, a neck lump, trouble swallowing, thirst or weight loss
Review in 6–8 weeks after dental care

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by chasing the stomach, by never looking in the mouth, and by missing the anxiety behind the visit. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Starting a PPI or requesting endoscopy for “stomach breath”.
items.why: Most halitosis is oral; he has no reflux or upper-GI symptoms.
items.fix: Look in the mouth first and explain the oral cause.

items.fail: Not looking at the tongue and gums or asking about the neck.
items.why: Tongue coating and gum disease are the common causes; an ulcer or neck lump would change the plan (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Look at tongue, gums, teeth, tonsils on video; ask her to feel her neck.

items.fail: Advising oral hygiene without mentioning the tongue or interdental cleaning.
items.why: Tongue coating is a major source and brushing alone misses it.
items.fix: Teach tongue and interdental cleaning alongside twice-daily brushing (OHID 2021).

items.fail: “See your dentist” with no idea how he will get an appointment.
items.why: Access is a real barrier; the advice may go nowhere.
items.fix: Explain he can book directly or use NHS 111 to find a dentist.

items.fail: Dismissing the problem because you cannot smell anything.
items.why: Misses real disease and the distress of halitophobia.
items.fix: Ask who has noticed it; explore checking and mood.

items.why: Non-healing ulcers or systemic symptoms need prompt action.
items.fix: Name the 3-week ulcer rule, neck lump, dysphagia, thirst and weight loss; review after dental care; teach-back.
